Tests for {@link BritishCutoverChronology} and its companion {@link BritishCutoverDate}.

The British calendar follows the Julian rules up to and including Wednesday 2nd September 1752, then jumps straight to Thursday 14th September 1752 under the Gregorian (ISO) rules. The 11 days from the 3rd to the 13th of September 1752 therefore never existed. Many test cases below probe the behaviour around this cutover gap, including the lenient handling of "dates" that fall inside it.

----------------------------------------------------------------------- creation, toLocalDate() ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Each row pairs a BritishCutoverDate with the ISO LocalDate that denotes the same point in time. Rows flagged "leniently accept invalid" sit inside the 1752 cutover gap, which the chronology tolerates rather than rejecting. Columns: { britishCutoverDate, equivalentIsoDate }
A date is always zero distance from itself.
The cutover date and its equivalent ISO date denote the same day, so the period is zero.
Same day in the other direction, so the ISO period is also zero.
Field combinations that do not form a valid date and must be rejected. Columns: { year, month, dayOfMonth }
2001 is not a leap year, so it has no 366th day.
Before the cutover the Julian rule applies: every fourth year is a leap year.
The first day on the Gregorian side of the gap: Thursday 14th September 1752.

----------------------------------------------------------------------- lengthOfMonth() ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Columns: { year, month, expectedLengthOfMonth } Note September 1752 has only 19 days because 11 days are removed by the cutover.
Proleptic years up to 0 belong to the BC era; 1 onwards to the AD era.
Building the same date from (era, year-of-era) must round-trip back.
Day-of-year 247 lands on the cutover date, skipping the removed days.
Only JulianEra values are accepted; an IsoEra must be rejected.

----------------------------------------------------------------------- BritishCutoverDate.with ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Setting a field on a starting date and asserting the resulting date. Rows flagged "lenient" produce a date inside the cutover gap, which is rolled forward rather than rejected. Columns: { year, month, dayOfMonth, field, newValue, expectedYear, expectedMonth, expectedDayOfMonth }
A bare Month cannot adjust a date in this chronology.

----------------------------------------------------------------------- BritishCutoverDate.plus ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Adding an amount of a unit to a starting date and asserting the result. The trailing "bidirectional" flag marks rows where subtracting the same amount from the expected date returns the starting date; it is consumed by test_minus_TemporalUnit. Columns: { year, month, dayOfMonth, amount, unit, expectedYear, expectedMonth, expectedDayOfMonth, bidirectional }
This reuses data_plus but swaps the start and expected columns: minus undoes plus. It only runs for rows whose plus operation is reversible (bidi == true).

----------------------------------------------------------------------- BritishCutoverDate.until ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Distance from one date to another measured in a single unit. Columns: { startYear, startMonth, startDay, endYear, endMonth, endDay, unit, expectedAmount }

----------------------------------------------------------------------- The full year/month/day period between two dates, and that adding it back reproduces the end. Inline comments on the rows explain how the cutover gap shifts the day count. Columns: { startYear, startMonth, startDay, endYear, endMonth, endDay, expectedYears, expectedMonths, expectedDays }
Adding the computed period back to the start must land exactly on the end date.
Round-trip through a plain LocalDateTime must preserve the date-time.
Walk every day from 1700 to 1800 in lock-step with a java.util GregorianCalendar that uses the same 1752 cutover, and assert that the two agree on every field.
